newsitem.title: INDONESIA: OPINION - Indonesian economy remains in track.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Indonesian economy remains in track.

text.p: By Felix D'Souza, head of research,
and Jason McCay, deputy head of research,
Peregrine Sewu Securities, Indonesia
JAKARTA, March 27 - The move taken by Bank Indonesia (BI) in mid-March to cut benchmark SBPU interest rates by 50 b.p. was the third central bank rate cut in three months.
Together with recent trade and inflation figures, the rate cut supports our view that the macroeconomic environment will remain positive for equity investors over the next six to 12 months.
Bank deposit rates should continue to trend down, GDP growth will remain strong and inflation and the current account are expected to stay within government and investor tolerance levels.
PLENTY OF GOOD NEWS FOR THE BANKS

We expect that BI will have to allow further falls in market interest rates in 1997 to slow down the more interest-rate- sensitive capital inflows, which continue to keep money supply growth at uncomfortably high levels.

Together with domestic credit control, a lower interest rate differential (slightly assisted by this week's 25 b.p. increase in the U.S. Fed rate) should help bring M2 growth down to a still robust 24 percent in 1997 (31 percent at the end of January 1997).

We expect 1997 rupiah depreciation to be slightly faster than in 1996 at 3.5 percent (2.3 percent in calendar year 1996). Bank deposit rates should fall by 100 b.p. from current levels in the next three-to-six months, but prime lending rates should remain relatively stable.
MORE UPSIDE FOR BANK STOCKS
After a healthy year-to-date market outperformance, the banking sector has corrected by seven percent over the past two weeks.
We continue to maintain an overweight position on the banks and see the current weakness as a buying opportunity.

Renewed concerns about Bank Indonesia strengthening its approach to "moral suasion" in order to curtail loan growth has provided an incentive to take profits ahead of the fiscal year end for many investors.
However, concerns about restrictions on loan growth are exaggerated whilst the sector's valuation is still attractive.
LARGE DISCOUNT TO MARKET

Although the market may now be familiar with the macro-economic reasons for owning bank shares, we believe that it is underestimating the impact of the attractive interest rate environment on sector profitability.
The banks are now trading on a prospective P/E of 11.8x, or an 18.2 percent discount to the market.
This relative valuation compares to historic valuation boundaries ranging from a 30 percent discount to a market rating.
STRONG EARNINGS GROWTH STILL EXPECTED
We expect strong relative earnings growth over the next two years of 27 percent, based on healthy loan growth and widening net interest margins.
Despite BI calls for total credit growth of only 17 percent in 1997, we forecast average loan growth for the listed banks in our coverage will be 26 percent in 1997, slowing to 23 percent in 1998.
LOAN GROWTH CONCERNS OVERSTATED

On the day that Bank Indonesia cut its benchmark SBPU rate by 50 basis points, bank officials had a meeting which was reported to have endorsed new restrictions on bank loan growth, to achieve BI's targeted 17 percent increase in lending.

We believe that the market has lost sight of the fact that BI's target is an average for the industry. BI will take into account the industry categories being lent to, a bank's credit quality, and its capital adequacy.
On these criteria, the listed private banks compared favourably with the state-owned banking sector, which is capital constrained and troubled with bad debts.
SLOW GROWTH AT STATE BANKS

Accounting for approximately 40 percent of industry assets, we expect state banks will continue to grow their loans by less than BI's targeted 17 percent, leaving room for private banks to expand at a faster rate.
As was the case in 1996, those banks with the cleanest balance sheets and best capital adequacy ratios will be given the greater leniency to exceed loan growth targets.

However, in 1997 it seems that the central bank has been particularly harsh on the banks with the largest loan books and those that exceeded 1996 targets by the greatest margin, that could have a greater impact on overall M2 growth.
Thus BII has officially been limited to loans growth of below 11 percent in 1997 -- although we expect this figure to be significantly exceeded.
INTEREST MARGINS TO WIDEN
We expect net interest margins to widen by 43 basis points this year, to 4.27 percent. This reflects our expectation for relatively stable lending rates combined with a declining cost of funds.

With three-month Bank Indonesia Certificates (SBIs) still yielding around 11.25 percent, we expect continued foreign inflows of hot money will drive deposit rates down by 100 basis points in 1997, more than compensating for the increased minimum reserve requirement.
This is reinforced by a change in the funding mix as most of the listed banks have recently undertaken rights issues boosting sector capital adequacy to 15 percent.
BUY BNI, BDNI
BNI has been one of the banks hardest hit by the recent sell off, declining by 18 percent over the past month.

Now trading on a 1997 P/E of 13.9x the stock offers good value for 34 percent compound annual earnings growth over the next two years. The bank has come in with a 23 percent y-y increase in 1996 net profit at Rp338.4b, 2.5 percent above Peregrine forecasts and 4.5 percent above consensus.

Bolstered by its Rp900b rights issue proceeds and the successful re-pricing of its commercial loan book in 4Q96, BDNI remains one of the cheapest stocks in the sector on 1997 P/E of 10.7x and 1.6x price/book.
(NOTE-The views expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters).
